## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Object Recognition and Computer Vision
  Official title       Object recognition and computer vision
  Instructors          G. VAROL, I. LAPTEV, J. PONCE, C. SCHMID, J. SIVIC, M. AUBRY, (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 30 h (lectures 30 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Computer Vision
  Language             English: all materials and lectures are in English; reports of the assignments and of the final project may be written in French or in English (master-mva.com)
  Assessment           Three programming assignments (50% of the grade) and a research-oriented final project, including a report and a presentation (50% of the grade) (master-mva.com) · Université Paris-Saclay: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment)
  Prerequisites        Basic linear algebra, analysis and probability (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who wants to understand, and to build, the systems that recognise objects, scenes and actions in photographs and videos.

**Empirical first**: photograph the same building from two street corners. Compared pixel by pixel, the two images look unrelated; yet a few hundred local feature matches, filtered by RANSAC, recover the geometric relation between the views in milliseconds. In 2012, a convolutional network cut the top-5 error of the ImageNet challenge from 26.2 % (the second-best entry) to 15.3 % (Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, 2012). This course explains both successes, and where each still fails.

The course goes from the geometry of a single camera to networks that learn from weak labels. It follows the official themes in order: instance-level recognition, category-level recognition, neural networks, convolutional networks, motion and actions, 3D objects and weak supervision.

It shares tools with [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [3D Computer Vision](../s1-3d-computer-vision/index.html) and [The Machine Intelligence of Images](../s1-machine-intelligence-images/index.html), taught in the same semester.

### What you will be able to do

-   Model image formation with the pinhole camera, and estimate cameras, homographies and fundamental matrices from point correspondences.
-   Detect corners and blobs (Harris, difference of Gaussians), describe them with SIFT, and prove which transformations each step is covariant or invariant to.
-   Match features robustly with the ratio test and RANSAC, and size RANSAC for a given outlier rate.
-   Build a large-scale visual search engine with visual words, inverted files and product quantisation.
-   Encode images with bags of features, spatial pyramids and sparse codes, and learn a dictionary.
-   Derive backpropagation, and train networks with stochastic gradient methods and a sound initialisation.
-   Design and analyse convolutional networks for classification and detection: receptive fields, equivariance, residual connections, IoU and non-maximum suppression.
-   Estimate optical flow, and explain the main families of action-recognition models.
-   Align 3D shapes (Kabsch, ICP), estimate an object pose from 2D–3D matches, and classify point clouds with a permutation-invariant network.
-   Learn localisation from image-level labels with multiple-instance learning and class activation maps, and explain contrastive and language supervision.
-   Read, reimplement and extend a recent computer vision paper, as the final project requires.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com presents automated object recognition — and, more generally, scene analysis — from photographs and videos as the great challenge of computer vision. Its objective is to give a coherent introductory overview of the image, object and scene models, and of the methods and algorithms, used today to address this challenge.

The same page announces 10 lectures of 3 hours each, with all materials and lectures in English, and lists seven themes. The Université Paris-Saclay course detail gives 30 h of lectures and an assessment type, and displays no list of contents. Each theme, and each part of a composite theme, has a row below.

| Official topic | Course section |

| Instance-level recognition: local-invariant features | [ch. 2](#ch2): covariance and invariance (Definition 2.1), Harris corners (Proposition 2.3), scale selection (Theorem 2.5), difference of Gaussians, SIFT (Algorithm 2.7, Proposition 2.8), affine regions |
| Instance-level recognition: correspondence | [ch. 3](#ch3): matching and the ratio test (Definition 3.1), RANSAC and its iteration count (Algorithm 3.3, Proposition 3.4), Hough voting (Definition 3.7) |
| Instance-level recognition: efficient visual search | [ch. 4](#ch4): visual words and k-means, tf-idf, inverted files, vocabulary trees, spatial re-ranking and query expansion, product quantisation (Definitions 4.1–4.7, Proposition 4.8) |
| Category-level recognition: bags of features | [ch. 5](#ch5): coding and pooling (Definition 5.1), histogram intersection kernel (Proposition 5.2), spatial pyramid matching (Definition 5.3), VLAD and Fisher vectors |

### Course outline

-   **Review: images, filters, least squares and gradient descent** — the four tools used everywhere else, with their short proofs.
-   **Camera geometry** — the pinhole camera, calibration, homographies, epipolar geometry and triangulation.
-   **Local invariant features** — Harris corners, scale space, scale selection, SIFT and affine regions.
-   **Correspondence and robust estimation** — matching, the ratio test, RANSAC and Hough voting.
-   **Efficient visual search** — visual words, inverted files, vocabulary trees and product quantisation.
-   **Category-level recognition** — bags of features, kernels, spatial pyramids, sparse coding and dictionary learning.
-   **Neural networks and optimisation methods** — backpropagation, stochastic gradient methods, initialisation and regularisation.
-   **Convolutional neural networks** — equivariance, receptive fields, residual networks, transfer, detection and segmentation.
-   **Motion and human actions** — optical flow and the families of action-recognition models.
-   **3D object recognition** — pose estimation, rigid alignment, point-cloud networks and recognition with 3D models.
-   **Weakly-supervised learning** — multiple-instance learning, weakly supervised detection, class activation maps, contrastive and language supervision.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — foundation models, geometry and learning, video and language (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read the chapters in order: each one uses only the previous ones, and ch. 0 can be skipped by a reader fluent in SVD and convolution.
-   After each session, do the exercises listed in its row of the session plan, then run the Python block of the chapter and change one parameter.
-   The Python environment is the one of the [scientific Python refresher](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html): NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and PyTorch on CPU. Every code block runs in less than 20 seconds on a laptop CPU, with synthetic data or the digits data set bundled with scikit-learn.
-   Start the final project early (see [Projects and assessment](#projects)): choose a paper after session 7, once the instance-level, category-level and deep learning tools are in place.
-   Keep a page of formulas: projection $P = K[R \mid t]$, epipolar constraint, RANSAC iteration count, receptive field recursion, Lucas–Kanade normal equations.

## 0. Review: images, filters, least squares and gradient descent {#ch0}

Every later chapter uses the same few tools: images as arrays, linear filtering, the singular value decomposition and gradient descent. This review states them once, with the short proofs that the course relies on.

The refreshers on [linear algebra and optimisation](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) and on [scientific Python](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) cover the same ground at a slower pace.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Digital image, convolution]{.tag}
A grey-level image is a function $I : \mathbb{Z}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$, stored as an $H \times W$ array; a colour image has three such channels. Positions are written $x = (x_1, x_2)$, row first.

The convolution of $I$ with a kernel $k$ of finite support is
$$
(I * k)(x) = \sum_{y \in \mathbb{Z}^2} I(x - y)\, k(y).
$$
Deep learning libraries implement the cross-correlation $\sum_y I(x + y)\, k(y)$, which is the convolution with the flipped kernel.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Linear shift-equivariant operators are convolutions]{.tag}
Let $\tau_a$ be the translation $(\tau_a I)(x) = I(x - a)$. Let $T$ be a linear operator on finitely supported images that commutes with every translation: $T \tau_a = \tau_a T$. Let $k = T\delta_0$ be its response to a unit impulse at the origin. Then
$$
T I = I * k \quad \text{for every image } I.
$$

::: proof
-   Write $I = \sum_y I(y)\, \delta_y$, where $\delta_y = \tau_y \delta_0$ is the impulse at $y$.
-   By linearity, $TI = \sum_y I(y)\, T\delta_y$.
-   By equivariance, $T\delta_y = \tau_y T\delta_0 = \tau_y k$, that is, $(T\delta_y)(x) = k(x - y)$.
-   Hence $(TI)(x) = \sum_y I(y)\, k(x - y)$, which is $(I * k)(x)$ after the change of variable $y \mapsto x - y$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This is why convolution is the natural first layer of a vision model: it is the only linear way to process every position of the image identically (ch. 7).

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Gaussian smoothing and image derivatives]{.tag}
The Gaussian kernel of scale $\sigma$ is
$$
G_\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2} \exp\Big(-\frac{\|x\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big).
$$
It is separable, a product of two one-dimensional Gaussians. It satisfies the semigroup property
$$
G_\sigma * G_\tau = G_{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \tau^2}},
$$
because the sum of two independent centred Gaussian vectors has the sum of their covariances.

Derivatives commute with convolution, $\partial_{1}(G_\sigma * I) = (\partial_{1} G_\sigma) * I$. Image gradients are therefore computed with *derivative-of-Gaussian* filters, which differentiate and denoise in one pass.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Homogeneous least squares]{.tag}
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ have the singular value decomposition $A = U \Sigma V^\top$, with singular values $\sigma_1 \geq \dots \geq \sigma_n \geq 0$ and right singular vectors $v_1, \dots, v_n$. Then
$$
\min_{\|x\| = 1} \|Ax\|^2 = \sigma_n^2, \quad \text{attained at } x = \pm v_n .
$$

When $m < n$, as for a minimal sample, the missing singular values are set to 0, and the minimum is 0.

::: proof
-   Write $x = \sum_i c_i v_i$; since $V$ is orthogonal, $\|x\| = 1$ means $\sum_i c_i^2 = 1$.
-   Since $A v_i = \sigma_i u_i$ with orthonormal $u_i$ (and $A v_i = 0$ for $i > m$), we get $\|Ax\|^2 = \sum_i \sigma_i^2 c_i^2$.
-   This weighted average of the $\sigma_i^2$ is at least $\sigma_n^2$, with equality for $c = \pm e_n$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Every estimation problem of ch. 1 — camera, homography, fundamental matrix, triangulation — reduces to this proposition. Stack one or two linear equations per correspondence into a matrix $A$, and take its last right singular vector.

::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Best low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young)]{.tag}
If $A = \sum_i \sigma_i u_i v_i^\top$, the matrix of rank at most $r$ closest to $A$ in Frobenius norm is the truncated sum
$$
A_r = \sum_{i \leq r} \sigma_i\, u_i v_i^\top .
$$
We use it to project an estimated fundamental matrix onto the matrices of rank 2 (ch. 1). A proof is in Golub and Van Loan (2013).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.6 — Descent lemma]{.tag}
Let $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable with an $L$-Lipschitz gradient. For all $\theta$ and $\theta'$,
$$
f(\theta') \leq f(\theta) + \nabla f(\theta)^\top (\theta' - \theta) + \frac{L}{2}\|\theta' - \theta\|^2 .
$$
Consequently, the gradient step $\theta^+ = \theta - \frac1L \nabla f(\theta)$ decreases $f$:
$$
f(\theta^+) \leq f(\theta) - \frac{1}{2L}\, \|\nabla f(\theta)\|^2 .
$$

::: proof
-   Let $h = \theta' - \theta$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus,
$$
f(\theta') - f(\theta) - \nabla f(\theta)^\top h = \int_0^1 \big(\nabla f(\theta + sh) - \nabla f(\theta)\big)^\top h \, ds .
$$
-   By Cauchy–Schwarz and the Lipschitz bound, the integrand is at most $L s \|h\|^2$, which integrates to $\frac{L}{2}\|h\|^2$.
-   Substituting $h = -\frac1L \nabla f(\theta)$ gives the second inequality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Sparse coding (ch. 5) and the analysis of stochastic gradient descent (ch. 6) both start from this inequality.

The three facts above can be checked numerically in a few lines.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
I = rng.random((64, 64))

# 1. Convolution commutes with (circular) translations
k = rng.random((5, 5))
conv = lambda img: ndimage.convolve(img, k, mode="wrap")
shift = lambda img: np.roll(img, (3, -2), axis=(0, 1))
print("equivariance error:", np.abs(conv(shift(I)) - shift(conv(I))).max())

# 2. Derivative-of-Gaussian gradient of a linear ramp 0.5 x + 0.25 y
y, x = np.mgrid[0:64, 0:64].astype(float)
ramp = 0.5 * x + 0.25 * y
gx = ndimage.gaussian_filter(ramp, 2.0, order=(0, 1))   # d/dx (along columns)
gy = ndimage.gaussian_filter(ramp, 2.0, order=(1, 0))   # d/dy (along rows)
print("gradient at the centre:", gx[32, 32].round(3), gy[32, 32].round(3))

# 3. Homogeneous least squares: minimise ||A x|| subject to ||x|| = 1
A = rng.normal(size=(20, 4))
x_true = np.array([1.0, -2.0, 0.5, 1.0]) / np.sqrt(6.25)
A -= np.outer(A @ x_true, x_true)           # x_true is now an exact null vector
A += 1e-3 * rng.normal(size=A.shape)        # small noise
_, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
x_hat = Vt[-1] * np.sign(Vt[-1] @ x_true)   # fix the sign ambiguity
print("smallest singular value:", s[-1].round(5))
print("error on x:", np.linalg.norm(x_hat - x_true).round(5))
```

The equivariance error is exactly zero, the filtered gradient of the ramp is $(0.5, 0.25)$, and the last right singular vector recovers the null vector to $2 \times 10^{-4}$.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 0
:::

-   Linear, shift-equivariant operators are exactly the convolutions (Proposition 0.2).
-   Image gradients are computed with derivative-of-Gaussian filters, and Gaussian blurs compose by adding variances.
-   Homogeneous least squares is solved by the last right singular vector (Proposition 0.4); rank constraints are imposed by truncating the SVD.
-   A gradient step of size $1/L$ decreases an $L$-smooth function by at least $\|\nabla f\|^2 / (2L)$.
::::

## 1. Camera geometry {#ch1}

Instance-level recognition asks whether *this* object — this book cover, this façade — appears in an image. A rigid object obeys the laws of perspective, so geometry gives the strongest test: a correct set of matches must be explained by a camera. This chapter builds the camera model and the constraints between two views.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Homogeneous coordinates]{.tag}
A point $(x, y)$ of the plane is represented by any vector $\lambda (x, y, 1)^\top$ with $\lambda \neq 0$. We write $\tilde{x} \sim (x, y, 1)^\top$ for equality up to a non-zero scale. Vectors $(x, y, 0)^\top$ represent *points at infinity*, that is, directions.

A line $\{ax + by + c = 0\}$ is the vector $l = (a, b, c)^\top$, and the point $\tilde{x}$ lies on $l$ if and only if
$$
l^\top \tilde{x} = 0 .
$$
The line through two points is $\tilde{x} \times \tilde{y}$, and the intersection of two lines is $l \times m$. Points of space use four homogeneous coordinates, $\tilde{X} \sim (X, Y, Z, 1)^\top$.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Pinhole camera]{.tag}
In the camera frame — centre at the origin, optical axis along $Z$ — a point $(X, Y, Z)$ with $Z > 0$ projects to $(fX/Z,\ fY/Z)$ on the image plane at focal distance $f$.

In pixel coordinates, with a world-to-camera rotation $R$ and translation $t$:
$$
\tilde{x} \sim P \tilde{X}, \qquad P = K\,[R \mid t], \qquad K = \begin{pmatrix} f_x & s & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
The matrix $K$ holds the *intrinsic* parameters: focal lengths in pixels, skew $s$ (usually 0) and principal point $(c_x, c_y)$.

$R$ and $t$ are the *extrinsic* parameters. The $3 \times 4$ matrix $P$ is defined up to scale and has 11 degrees of freedom.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.3 — Projecting by hand]{.tag}
Take $f_x = f_y = 800$ px, the principal point $(320, 240)$, zero skew, and the point $(0.5, -0.2, 4)$, in metres, in the camera frame.

-   $u = 800 \times 0.5 / 4 + 320 = 420$.
-   $v = 800 \times (-0.2) / 4 + 240 = 200$.

Moving the point to depth 8 m halves its offset from the principal point:
$$
(420, 200) \ \longrightarrow\ (370, 220).
$$
This $1/Z$ shrinking is why the apparent size of an object says nothing about its true size without knowing its depth.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.4 — Camera centre and vanishing points]{.tag}
Let $P = K[R \mid t]$ with $K$ invertible.

1.  The camera centre $C = -R^\top t$ spans the kernel of $P$: $P\,(C^\top, 1)^\top = 0$.
2.  All lines of space with direction $d$ project to image lines through a common point, the *vanishing point*
$$
\tilde{v} \sim K R\, d .
$$

::: proof
1.  $P (C^\top, 1)^\top = K(RC + t) = K(-t + t) = 0$, and $P$ has rank 3, so its kernel has dimension one.
2.  A point $X_0 + \lambda d$ of the line has homogeneous coordinates proportional to $(X_0/\lambda + d,\ 1/\lambda)$, which tend to $(d, 0)$ as $\lambda \to \infty$. Their images tend to $P(d^\top, 0)^\top = KRd$, whatever $X_0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Vanishing points calibrate a camera from a single image of a building. With zero skew and square pixels, the principal point is the orthocentre of the triangle formed by the vanishing points of three orthogonal directions, and the focal length follows (Hartley and Zisserman, 2004).

::: thm
[Algorithm 1.5 — Calibration by the direct linear transform]{.tag}
Input: $n \geq 6$ correspondences $X_i \leftrightarrow x_i$ between known 3D points of a calibration object, not all on one plane, and their images. For coplanar points the system below is degenerate; a planar target is handled by the homography method described after the algorithm.

1.  Normalise the coordinates with similarities $T$ (image) and $T_3$ (space) that centre each point set and scale its mean distance to $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt3$.
2.  Each correspondence gives, through $\tilde{x}_i \times P\tilde{X}_i = 0$, two independent linear equations in the 12 entries of $P$.

    Stack them into $Ap = 0$, with $A$ of size $2n \times 12$, and take for $p$ the last right singular vector of $A$ (Proposition 0.4). Undo the normalisation: $P = T^{-1} \hat{P}\, T_3$.
3.  Factor the left $3 \times 3$ block of $P$ as $KR$ by an RQ decomposition, with a positive diagonal for $K$ and the sign of $P$ chosen so that $\det R = 1$.

    Then $t = K^{-1} p_4$, where $p_4$ is the last column of $P$.
4.  Refine all the parameters, together with lens distortion, by minimising the reprojection error $\sum_i \|x_i - \pi(P\tilde{X}_i)\|^2$ with the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm, where $\pi$ divides by the third coordinate.
:::

In practice one films a planar checkerboard in several positions (Zhang, 2000). Each view gives a homography between the board and the image, and each homography gives two linear constraints on $K$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.6 — When two views are related by a homography]{.tag}
A homography is an invertible $3 \times 3$ matrix $H$ acting on homogeneous image points, defined up to scale; it has 8 degrees of freedom.

1.  The images of a *plane* that contains neither camera centre are related by a homography, $\tilde{x}' \sim H \tilde{x}$.
2.  Two views taken from the *same centre*, by a camera rotating about its optical centre, are related for every scene point by
$$
H = K' R\, K^{-1} .
$$

::: proof
1.  Choose world coordinates in which the plane is $Z = 0$, and let $r_1, r_2$ be the first two columns of $R$.
    -   A point $(X, Y, 0)$ of the plane projects to $K[r_1\ r_2\ t]\,(X, Y, 1)^\top$.
    -   So the map from the plane to the image is the $3 \times 3$ matrix $H_1 = K[r_1\ r_2\ t]$, invertible when the plane does not contain the camera centre.
    -   With $H_2$ the analogous matrix of the second camera, $\tilde{x}' \sim H_2 H_1^{-1} \tilde{x}$.
2.  Put the common centre at the origin and take the axes of the first camera as world axes.
    -   Then $\tilde{x} \sim K X$ and $\tilde{x}' \sim K' R X$ for every point $X$.
    -   Eliminating $X \sim K^{-1}\tilde{x}$ gives $\tilde{x}' \sim K' R K^{-1} \tilde{x}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Part 1 is why a book cover, a painting or a façade can be verified with a homography. Part 2 is the basis of panorama stitching.

::: thm
[Algorithm 1.7 — Estimating a homography (normalised DLT)]{.tag}
From $n \geq 4$ correspondences $x_i \leftrightarrow y_i$:

1.  Compute similarities $T$ and $T'$ that centre each point set and scale its mean distance to the centroid to $\sqrt{2}$ (Hartley's normalisation).
2.  Each normalised correspondence gives two rows of the equation $\tilde{y} \times H\tilde{x} = 0$. Stack them in a $2n \times 9$ matrix and take its last right singular vector as $\hat{H}$.
3.  Undo the normalisation: $H = T'^{-1} \hat{H}\, T$.
:::

Without step 1, pixel coordinates of order $10^3$ make the columns of the system differ by six orders of magnitude, and the solution becomes very sensitive to noise (Hartley, 1997). The code fits a homography to 50 correspondences corrupted by 0.5 px of noise.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
np.set_printoptions(suppress=True, precision=4)

def normalise(p):
    """Similarity T: centroid to 0, mean distance to sqrt(2) (Hartley)."""
    c = p.mean(0)
    s = np.sqrt(2) / np.linalg.norm(p - c, axis=1).mean()
    return np.array([[s, 0, -s * c[0]], [0, s, -s * c[1]], [0, 0, 1]])

def dlt_homography(x, y):
    """H with y ~ H x from n >= 4 correspondences (n x 2 arrays)."""
    Tx, Ty = normalise(x), normalise(y)
    xh = np.c_[x, np.ones(len(x))] @ Tx.T
    yh = np.c_[y, np.ones(len(y))] @ Ty.T
    rows = []
    for (a, b, c), (u, v, w) in zip(xh, yh):      # two rows of y x (H x) = 0
        rows.append([0, 0, 0, -w*a, -w*b, -w*c, v*a, v*b, v*c])
        rows.append([w*a, w*b, w*c, 0, 0, 0, -u*a, -u*b, -u*c])
    h = np.linalg.svd(np.array(rows))[2][-1]       # Proposition 0.4
    H = np.linalg.inv(Ty) @ h.reshape(3, 3) @ Tx   # undo the normalisation
    return H / H[2, 2]

def apply(H, x):
    p = np.c_[x, np.ones(len(x))] @ H.T
    return p[:, :2] / p[:, 2:]

H_true = np.array([[1.1, 0.05, 30], [-0.08, 0.95, 12], [2e-4, -1e-4, 1]])
x = rng.uniform(0, 640, size=(50, 2))
y = apply(H_true, x) + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=(50, 2))   # 0.5 px noise
H = dlt_homography(x, y)
err = np.linalg.norm(apply(H, x) - y, axis=1)
print("estimated H:\n", H)
print("mean reprojection error (px):", err.mean().round(3))
```

The mean residual is 0.59 px. For two-dimensional Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.5 px per coordinate, the mean distance is $0.5\sqrt{\pi/2} \approx 0.63$ px: the fit is as good as the data allow.

::: def
[Definition 1.8 — Epipolar geometry]{.tag}
Two cameras with distinct centres $C$ and $C'$ observe a point $X$. The *baseline* $CC'$ and the point $X$ span the *epipolar plane* of $X$.

-   The *epipoles* $e$ and $e'$ are the images of each camera centre in the other view.
-   The *epipolar line* of $x$ in the second view is the intersection of the epipolar plane with the second image plane. It passes through $e'$ and contains the match $x'$.

Searching for the match of a point therefore reduces from a 2D search to a 1D search along a line.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.9 — Essential and fundamental matrices]{.tag}
Let the cameras be $P = K[I \mid 0]$ and $P' = K'[R \mid t]$, and let $[t]_\times$ be the matrix of the map $v \mapsto t \times v$. Define
$$
E = [t]_\times R, \qquad F = K'^{-\top} E\, K^{-1} .
$$
Then every pair of matching image points satisfies the *epipolar constraint*:

::: key
[Key result — the epipolar constraint]{.tag}
$$
\tilde{x}'^\top F\, \tilde{x} = 0 .
$$
:::

Moreover $F$ has rank 2, $Fe = 0$ and $F^\top e' = 0$, and the epipolar line of $x$ in the second view is $l' = F\tilde{x}$.

::: proof
-   Let $\hat{x} = K^{-1}\tilde{x}$ and $\hat{x}' = K'^{-1}\tilde{x}'$ be the normalised coordinates. In the two camera frames, the scene point is $X = \lambda \hat{x}$ and $X' = RX + t = \lambda' \hat{x}'$, with depths $\lambda, \lambda' > 0$.
-   The vectors $X'$, $t$ and $RX$ lie in one plane, since $X' = RX + t$.

    So $X'$ is orthogonal to $t \times RX$, that is, $X'^\top [t]_\times R X = 0$.
-   Dividing by $\lambda\lambda'$ gives $\hat{x}'^\top E \hat{x} = 0$; substituting the normalised coordinates gives the constraint on $F$.
-   $[t]_\times$ has rank 2, its kernel being spanned by $t$, while $R$, $K$ and $K'$ are invertible: $F$ has rank 2.
-   The first epipole is the image of $C' = -R^\top t$, so $e \sim K R^\top t$ and $Fe \sim K'^{-\top} [t]_\times t = 0$. The case of $e'$ is symmetric. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Algorithm 1.10 — The normalised eight-point algorithm]{.tag}
1.  Normalise both point sets as in Algorithm 1.7.
2.  Each correspondence gives one linear equation $\tilde{x}'^\top F \tilde{x} = 0$ in the 9 entries of $F$. With $n \geq 8$ matches, take the last right singular vector of the $n \times 9$ system (Proposition 0.4).
3.  Enforce rank 2 by setting the smallest singular value of the estimate to zero (Proposition 0.5), then undo the normalisation: $F = T'^\top \hat{F}\, T$.
:::

With calibrated cameras, $E$ has 5 degrees of freedom and two equal non-zero singular values (Exercise 9). Five correspondences then suffice (Nistér, 2004), which matters inside RANSAC (ch. 3).

::: prop
[Proposition 1.11 — Linear triangulation]{.tag}
Given $P$, $P'$ and a match $x \leftrightarrow x'$, each of the conditions $\tilde{x} \times P\tilde{X} = 0$ and $\tilde{x}' \times P'\tilde{X} = 0$ gives two independent linear equations in $\tilde{X} \in \mathbb{R}^4$.

The stacked $4 \times 4$ system has rank 3 for exact data, and its least-squares solution is the last right singular vector (Proposition 0.4).
:::

With noise, the two back-projected rays do not meet. The statistically optimal estimate minimises the reprojection error in both images. Refining all cameras and all points jointly in this way is *bundle adjustment*, the core of structure from motion (Snavely, Seitz and Szeliski, 2006).

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::

-   A camera is the projective map $P = K[R \mid t]$; its centre spans the kernel of $P$, and parallel lines meet at the vanishing point $KRd$.
-   Views of a plane, and views from a rotating camera, are related by a homography (Theorem 1.6).
-   General pairs of views obey the epipolar constraint $\tilde{x}'^\top F \tilde{x} = 0$, with $F$ of rank 2 (Theorem 1.9).
-   Cameras, homographies and fundamental matrices are estimated linearly by SVD after Hartley's normalisation, then refined by minimising the reprojection error.
::::

## 2. Local invariant features {#ch2}

Two photographs of the same object differ by viewpoint, scale, rotation, lighting and occlusion. Local features sidestep most of these nuisances: detect many small distinctive regions in a *covariant* way, describe each one by an *invariant* vector, and match the vectors.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Covariant detector, invariant descriptor]{.tag}
Let $g$ be a transformation of the image plane, such as a rotation, a scaling or an affine map.

-   A detector is *covariant* if, whenever it detects the region $R$ in $I$, it detects $g(R)$ in the transformed image $I \circ g^{-1}$.
-   A descriptor $\phi$ is *invariant* if it gives the same vector for corresponding regions:
$$
\phi\big(g(R),\, I \circ g^{-1}\big) = \phi(R, I).
$$

Covariance of the detector makes regions *repeatable*; invariance of the descriptor makes them *matchable*.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — Structure tensor]{.tag}
For an image $I$ with gradient $\nabla I$ and a Gaussian window $w$ centred at $x_0$, the structure tensor, or second-moment matrix, is
$$
M = \sum_x w(x - x_0)\, \nabla I(x)\, \nabla I(x)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}.
$$
It is symmetric positive semi-definite, with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq 0$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Harris corners]{.tag}
Let $E(h) = \sum_x w(x - x_0)\,\big(I(x + h) - I(x)\big)^2$ measure how much the window changes under a small shift $h$.

1.  To second order, $E(h) \approx h^\top M h$. The window changes in every direction iff $\lambda_2$ is large: a *corner*. One large eigenvalue means an *edge*, two small ones a *flat* region.
2.  The Harris response, with $\kappa \in [0.04, 0.06]$,
$$
R = \det M - \kappa\, (\operatorname{tr} M)^2 = \lambda_1\lambda_2 - \kappa\,(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)^2,
$$
is invariant to rotations of the image about $x_0$.

::: proof
1.  The Taylor expansion $I(x + h) - I(x) = \nabla I(x)^\top h + O(\|h\|^2)$ gives $E(h) = h^\top M h + O(\|h\|^3)$. Over unit vectors $h$, the minimum and maximum of $h^\top M h$ are $\lambda_2$ and $\lambda_1$.
2.  Take $x_0 = 0$ and $J = I \circ Q^\top$ for a rotation $Q$. The chain rule gives $\nabla J(Qx) = Q \nabla I(x)$. Since the Gaussian window is radial, the change of variable $y = Qx$ gives $M_J = Q M_I Q^\top$. This matrix has the same eigenvalues, hence the same determinant and trace. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The code detects corners on a synthetic image of two rectangles.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

# Synthetic image: two bright rectangles on a dark background
I = np.zeros((100, 100))
I[20:50, 20:50] = 1.0
I[60:85, 55:90] = 1.0

def harris(I, sigma_d=1.0, sigma_i=2.0, kappa=0.05):
    Ix = ndimage.gaussian_filter(I, sigma_d, order=(0, 1))
    Iy = ndimage.gaussian_filter(I, sigma_d, order=(1, 0))
    Sxx = ndimage.gaussian_filter(Ix * Ix, sigma_i)    # entries of the structure tensor
    Syy = ndimage.gaussian_filter(Iy * Iy, sigma_i)
    Sxy = ndimage.gaussian_filter(Ix * Iy, sigma_i)
    return Sxx * Syy - Sxy**2 - kappa * (Sxx + Syy)**2

R = harris(I)
peaks = (R == ndimage.maximum_filter(R, size=7)) & (R > 0.1 * R.max())
print("corners (row, col):", np.argwhere(peaks).tolist())
print("response on an edge / in a flat zone:", R[35, 20].round(5), R[5, 5].round(5))

# Scale selection: scale-normalised Laplacian at the centre of a Gaussian blob of std 4
yy, xx = np.mgrid[-50:51, -50:51]
blob = np.exp(-(xx**2 + yy**2) / (2 * 4.0**2))
sigmas = np.linspace(1, 10, 91)
resp = [-(s**2) * ndimage.gaussian_laplace(blob, s)[50, 50] for s in sigmas]
print("selected scale:", sigmas[int(np.argmax(resp))].round(2))
```

The detector returns the eight corners, each one pixel inside the rectangle. The response is negative on the edges and zero in flat zones, as Proposition 2.3 predicts.

The Harris detector is not covariant to scaling: a sharp corner seen from far away becomes a rounded curve when the image is enlarged. Scale covariance needs a representation of the image at all scales.

::: def
[Definition 2.4 — Gaussian scale space]{.tag}
The scale space of $I$ is the family of blurred images $L(\cdot, \sigma) = G_\sigma * I$, for $\sigma > 0$. It solves the heat equation
$$
\partial_\sigma L = \sigma\, \Delta L ,
$$
and by the semigroup property (Definition 0.3) coarse scales can be computed from fine ones. Derivatives are compared across scales after *normalisation*: $\sigma^2 \Delta L$ is the scale-normalised Laplacian.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.5 — Automatic scale selection (Lindeberg, 1998)]{.tag}
Let $I = G_s$ be a Gaussian blob of size $s$. At its centre, the scale-normalised Laplacian response
$$
\sigma \mapsto \sigma^2\, |\Delta L(0, \sigma)|
$$
is maximal exactly at $\sigma = s$.

More generally, let $I'(x) = I(x/c)$ be a copy of the image enlarged by a factor $c$. Every extremum at $(x, \sigma)$ for the original image corresponds to an extremum at $(cx, c\sigma)$ for $I'$: scale selection is covariant.

::: proof
-   By the semigroup property, $L(\cdot, \sigma) = G_s * G_\sigma = G_\tau$ with $\tau^2 = s^2 + \sigma^2$.
-   Differentiating the Gaussian twice,
$$
\Delta G_\tau(x) = G_\tau(x)\,\Big(\frac{\|x\|^2}{\tau^4} - \frac{2}{\tau^2}\Big), \qquad \Delta G_\tau(0) = -\frac{1}{\pi \tau^4} .
$$
-   With $u = \sigma^2$, the response is $\varphi(u) = u / \big(\pi (s^2 + u)^2\big)$, and
$$
\varphi'(u) = \frac{s^2 - u}{\pi\, (s^2 + u)^3} .
$$
It is positive for $u < s^2$ and negative after, so the maximum is at $\sigma = s$, with value $1/(4\pi s^2)$.
-   For the enlarged image, the change of variable $x = cy$ in the convolution gives $L'(cy, c\sigma) = L(y, \sigma)$. Second derivatives in $x$ carry a factor $c^{-2}$, which the normalisation $(c\sigma)^2$ exactly compensates. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.6 — Difference of Gaussians]{.tag}
For $k > 1$ close to 1,
$$
G_{k\sigma} - G_\sigma \approx (k - 1)\, \sigma^2\, \Delta G_\sigma .
$$
The difference of two consecutive levels of a Gaussian pyramid therefore approximates the scale-normalised Laplacian, up to the constant factor $k - 1$, at the cost of one subtraction.

::: proof
The heat equation of Definition 2.4 gives $\partial_\sigma G_\sigma = \sigma \Delta G_\sigma$, and a first-order expansion in $\sigma$ gives
$$
G_{k\sigma} - G_\sigma \approx (k\sigma - \sigma)\, \sigma\Delta G_\sigma = (k - 1)\,\sigma^2\, \Delta G_\sigma .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Algorithm 2.7 — SIFT (Lowe, 2004)]{.tag}
1.  **Detection.** Build a Gaussian pyramid with three scales per octave ($k = 2^{1/3}$), take differences of consecutive levels, and keep the extrema over the 26 neighbours in position and scale.
2.  **Refinement.** Fit a quadratic to locate each extremum to sub-pixel and sub-scale accuracy. Reject points of low contrast, and edge points whose Hessian $H$ has a ratio of principal curvatures above $r = 10$, that is, $\operatorname{tr}(H)^2 / \det H > (r + 1)^2 / r$.
3.  **Orientation.** Build a 36-bin histogram of gradient orientations around the point, weighted by gradient magnitude, and assign its peak as the orientation. Secondary peaks above 80 % of the maximum create additional keypoints.
4.  **Descriptor.** In the frame given by the position, scale and orientation, a $4 \times 4$ grid of 8-bin orientation histograms gives a 128-dimensional vector. Normalise it to unit length, clip its entries at 0.2, and normalise again.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.8 — Invariances of the SIFT descriptor]{.tag}
The descriptor is invariant to rotations and scalings of the image, because it is computed in the frame given by the detected orientation and scale. It is also invariant to affine changes of intensity $I \mapsto aI + b$ with $a > 0$.

::: proof
The constant $b$ disappears in the gradient. The factor $a$ leaves gradient orientations unchanged and multiplies every histogram entry by $a$, which the normalisation to unit length removes. The clipping is applied after this normalisation, so the whole descriptor is unchanged. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Clipping limits the influence of a few large gradients, caused for instance by saturation, which the affine model of intensity does not cover.

::: ex
[Example 2.9 — Scale selection in numbers]{.tag}
In the code above, a Gaussian blob of standard deviation 4 px is detected at the scale
$$
\sigma = 4.0 .
$$
After downsampling by 2, the same blob has size 2 px and is detected at $\sigma = 2$. The descriptor window, proportional to $\sigma$, covers the same part of the object in both images: this is the covariance required by Definition 2.1.
:::

::: note
[Affine regions and learned features]{.tag}
Under a strong change of viewpoint, a small planar patch undergoes an affine map, not a similarity. Harris-Affine and Hessian-Affine detectors (Mikolajczyk and Schmid, 2004) iterate scale selection and a transformation of the local frame by $M^{1/2}$, until the structure tensor of the patch becomes isotropic. Detectors and descriptors are now also learned end to end, for instance SuperPoint (DeTone, Malisiewicz and Rabinovich, 2018); ch. 11 returns to them.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::

-   Detectors must be covariant and descriptors invariant to the transformations between views (Definition 2.1).
-   The structure tensor $M$ classifies corners, edges and flat regions; the Harris response is rotation invariant.
-   Scale is selected at the extrema of the scale-normalised Laplacian (Theorem 2.5), which a difference of Gaussians approximates cheaply.
-   SIFT combines DoG detection, a dominant orientation and a normalised 128-dimensional histogram of gradients, invariant to similarity transforms and affine intensity changes.
::::

## 3. Correspondence and robust estimation {#ch3}

Matching descriptors gives *putative* correspondences, a large fraction of which are wrong: repeated textures, occlusions and features without a counterpart all produce false matches. This chapter turns putative matches into a verified geometric relation.

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Matching strategies]{.tag}
For a descriptor $d$ of the first image, let $d_1$ and $d_2$ be its nearest and second-nearest neighbours among the descriptors of the second image.

-   *Nearest neighbour*: accept $d \leftrightarrow d_1$.
-   *Mutual nearest neighbours*: also require $d$ to be the nearest neighbour of $d_1$.
-   *Ratio test* (Lowe, 2004): accept only if
$$
\frac{\|d - d_1\|}{\|d - d_2\|} < \rho, \qquad \rho \approx 0.8 .
$$

The ratio test measures distinctiveness: a feature on a repeated pattern has a close second neighbour and is rejected. Lowe reports that $\rho = 0.8$ eliminates 90 % of the false matches while discarding less than 5 % of the correct ones.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Least squares does not survive outliers]{.tag}
Fit a translation $a$ to matches $x_i \leftrightarrow y_i$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, by minimising $\sum_i \|y_i - x_i - a\|^2$. The solution is the mean displacement
$$
\hat{a} = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - x_i),
$$
so a single wrong match displaced by $D$ moves $\hat{a}$ by $D/n$, without bound as $D$ grows.

::: proof
The objective is a convex quadratic in $a$, with gradient $-2\sum_i (y_i - x_i - a)$; it vanishes at $\hat{a}$. Replacing one displacement by another one at distance $D$ changes the mean by $D/n$ in norm. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The *breakdown point* of least squares is therefore 0: an arbitrarily small fraction of outliers can make the estimate arbitrarily bad. The code at the end of this chapter shows the same failure for a homography.

::: thm
[Algorithm 3.3 — RANSAC (Fischler and Bolles, 1981)]{.tag}
Input: $n$ putative matches, a model that can be fitted to minimal samples of size $s$ (4 for a homography, 7 or 8 for a fundamental matrix), and an inlier threshold $t$.

1.  Draw a random minimal sample and fit the model to it.
2.  Count the *inliers*, the matches whose residual is below $t$.
3.  Keep the model with the largest inlier set, and repeat for $N$ iterations.
4.  Refit the model by least squares on all the inliers of the best model.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — How many RANSAC iterations?]{.tag}
Let $w$ be the fraction of inliers, and draw samples independently. The probability that at least one of $N$ samples contains only inliers is $1 - (1 - w^s)^N$. It exceeds a confidence level $p$ as soon as

::: key
[Key result — the number of RANSAC iterations]{.tag}
$$
N \geq \frac{\log(1 - p)}{\log(1 - w^s)} .
$$
:::


::: proof
-   A sample is free of outliers with probability $w^s$ when drawing with replacement; without replacement the probability is slightly smaller for small $n$.
-   The $N$ independent samples all fail with probability $(1 - w^s)^N$.
-   Take logarithms in $(1 - w^s)^N \leq 1 - p$, and divide by the negative number $\log(1 - w^s)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.5 — Sizing RANSAC]{.tag}
For a confidence $p = 0.99$, the minimal number of iterations is:

| Model | $s$ | $w = 0.7$ | $w = 0.5$ | $w = 0.3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| line, or similarity from 2 points | 2 | 7 | 17 | 49 |
| homography | 4 | 17 | 72 | 567 |
| fundamental matrix, 7 points | 7 | 54 | 588 | 21 055 |
| fundamental matrix, 8 points | 8 | 78 | 1 177 | 70 188 |

The cost grows exponentially with $s$, which is why minimal solvers such as the seven-point and five-point algorithms matter. Since $w$ is unknown, implementations update $N$ each time a larger inlier set is found.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — Choosing the threshold]{.tag}
Assume the points $x$ of the first image are exact, and the inlier positions $y$ in the second image carry independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation $\sigma$ on each coordinate. With the true model, the squared transfer error $e^2 = \|y - H(x)\|^2$ is then distributed as $\sigma^2 \chi^2_2$, the sum of two squared standard Gaussians. A threshold that keeps 95 % of the inliers is therefore
$$
t^2 = 5.99\, \sigma^2 ,
$$
since 5.99 is the 0.95 quantile of the $\chi^2_2$ law. When both images are noisy, the same quantile applies to the reprojection error of the optimal correction (Hartley and Zisserman, 2004, ch. 4).
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Hough voting]{.tag}
A match between two features with position, scale and orientation determines, on its own, a similarity transformation with 4 parameters. Each match *votes* for its transformation in a coarse 4D histogram. Bins with many votes give groups of mutually consistent matches, which are then verified by fitting an affine transformation (Lowe, 2004).

Voting costs $O(n)$ and tolerates a much larger fraction of outliers than RANSAC with 4-point samples, which would need about 46 000 iterations at $w = 0.1$.
:::

The code runs RANSAC on 200 matches, half of which are outliers, and compares it with a least-squares fit on all matches.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

def dlt(x, y):                       # minimal DLT (coordinates already in [0, 1])
    A = []
    for (a, b), (u, v) in zip(x, y):
        A.append([0, 0, 0, -a, -b, -1, v*a, v*b, v])
        A.append([a, b, 1, 0, 0, 0, -u*a, -u*b, -u])
    H = np.linalg.svd(np.array(A))[2][-1].reshape(3, 3)
    return H / H[2, 2]

def apply(H, x):
    p = np.c_[x, np.ones(len(x))] @ H.T
    return p[:, :2] / p[:, 2:]

def ransac(x, y, thresh, p=0.99, max_iter=10_000):
    best, N, it = np.zeros(len(x), bool), max_iter, 0
    while it < N:
        idx = rng.choice(len(x), 4, replace=False)          # minimal sample
        inliers = np.linalg.norm(apply(dlt(x[idx], y[idx]), x) - y, axis=1) < thresh
        if inliers.sum() > best.sum():
            best, w = inliers, inliers.mean()
            N = min(max_iter, np.log(1 - p) / np.log(1 - w**4 + 1e-12))  # Prop. 3.4
        it += 1
    for _ in range(3):                                       # refit on all inliers, re-classify
        H = dlt(x[best], y[best])
        best = np.linalg.norm(apply(H, x) - y, axis=1) < thresh
    return H, best, it

# 200 putative matches, 50 % outliers, 1 px noise at a 640 px image scale
H_true = np.array([[1.05, 0.1, 0.05], [-0.05, 0.9, 0.1], [0.2, -0.1, 1.0]])
x = rng.uniform(0, 1, (200, 2))
y = apply(H_true, x) + rng.normal(scale=1 / 640, size=(200, 2))
outlier = rng.random(200) < 0.5
y[outlier] = rng.uniform(0, 1, (outlier.sum(), 2))
H, inl, iters = ransac(x, y, thresh=np.sqrt(5.99) / 640)
print("iterations:", iters, "| inliers kept:", inl.sum(), "| true inliers:", (~outlier).sum())
print("false inliers:", (inl & outlier).sum(), "| max |H - H_true|:", np.abs(H - H_true).max().round(4))
H_ls = dlt(x, y)                                             # plain least squares on all matches
print("least squares on all matches, max |H - H_true|:", np.abs(H_ls - H_true).max().round(2))
```

RANSAC keeps 91 of the 97 true inliers, about the 95 % expected from Proposition 3.6, and accepts no outlier. It runs 437 iterations rather than the 72 of Example 3.5: a model fitted to four noisy points finds fewer inliers than the true model. The best minimal model has 64 inliers, so the running estimate is $w = 0.32$ instead of 0.49. The least-squares fit on all matches is useless, with entries off by 1.76.

::: note
[Beyond the basic loop]{.tag}
PROSAC draws the most distinctive matches first (Chum and Matas, 2005). LO-RANSAC re-estimates the model from the current inliers inside the loop (Chum, Matas and Kittler, 2003); the three refits at the end of the code are a crude version of it. Finally, M-estimators replace the square by a robust loss such as Huber's, and are solved by iteratively reweighted least squares from the RANSAC estimate.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::

-   The ratio test keeps distinctive matches; geometry must still remove the remaining false ones.
-   Least squares has breakdown point 0; RANSAC tolerates a majority of outliers.
-   RANSAC needs $\log(1 - p) / \log(1 - w^s)$ iterations, exponential in the sample size $s$ (Proposition 3.4).
-   The inlier threshold follows from the noise level through the $\chi^2_2$ law; Hough voting is a linear-time alternative for large outlier rates.
-   Instance-level recognition accepts an object when enough matches are geometrically verified.
::::

## 4. Efficient visual search {#ch4}

Matching a query image against one database image costs about $10^6$ descriptor comparisons, with 1 000 features on each side. Against a million images, that is $10^{12}$ comparisons per query. Large-scale search borrows the tools of text retrieval (Sivic and Zisserman, 2003): quantise descriptors into *visual words*, index the words, and verify geometry only for the best candidates.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Visual vocabulary]{.tag}
A vocabulary is a set of $K$ centroids $c_1, \dots, c_K \in \mathbb{R}^d$, learned by k-means on descriptors $x_1, \dots, x_N$ of training images. It minimises
$$
J(c, a) = \sum_{i=1}^N \|x_i - c_{a_i}\|^2, \qquad a_i \in \{1, \dots, K\}.
$$
The quantiser maps a descriptor to its nearest centroid, its *visual word*; the cells of the quantiser are the Voronoi regions of the centroids.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Lloyd's algorithm decreases the k-means objective]{.tag}
Alternate (i) assigning each $x_i$ to its nearest centroid and (ii) replacing each centroid by the mean of its assigned points. Then $J$ never increases, and it is constant after finitely many iterations.

::: proof
-   Step (i) minimises $J$ over the assignment $a$ for fixed centroids, term by term.
-   Step (ii) minimises $J$ over $c$ for a fixed assignment: the gradient of $c \mapsto \sum_{i \in S}\|x_i - c\|^2$ is $2\sum_{i \in S}(c - x_i)$, which vanishes at the mean.
-   So $J$ is non-increasing. It takes finitely many values, one per assignment, so it is eventually constant. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — Bag of visual words and tf-idf]{.tag}
Let image $d$ have $n_d$ features, of which $n_{wd}$ are quantised to the word $w$.

Among the $N$ database images, let $N_w$ contain the word $w$. The image is represented by the vector of weights
$$
t_{wd} = \frac{n_{wd}}{n_d}\, \log\frac{N}{N_w} .
$$
The first factor is the *term frequency*. The second, the *inverse document frequency*, down-weights frequent and uninformative words. Images are ranked by the cosine similarity of their normalised vectors, and the most frequent words are often removed altogether (a *stop list*).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.4 — Cost of an inverted file]{.tag}
An inverted file stores, for each word $w$, the list of the $N_w$ images that contain it, with their weights. Scoring a query touches only the lists of its own words:
$$
\text{cost} = \sum_{w \in \text{query}} N_w .
$$
Assume $N$ images with $n$ features each, spread evenly over $K$ words. A list then holds about $Nn/K$ entries.

A query with $q$ words therefore costs about $qNn/K$ operations, against $qNn$ descriptor comparisons for exhaustive matching: a speed-up of order $K$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.5 — A million images]{.tag}
Take $N = 10^6$ images with $n = 10^3$ features each, and $K = 10^6$ words.

-   Exhaustive matching: $10^3 \times 10^9 = 10^{12}$ descriptor distances per query.
-   Inverted file: about $Nn/K = 10^3$ entries per list, so about $10^6$ score updates per query.

The reduction by a factor of a million is what made search in feature films and in large photo collections interactive (Sivic and Zisserman, 2003; Nistér and Stewénius, 2006).
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Vocabulary tree]{.tag}
Quantising into $10^6$ words by brute force costs $10^6$ distance computations per descriptor. A *vocabulary tree* (Nistér and Stewénius, 2006) applies k-means with a small branching factor $b$ recursively, down to depth $L$:
$$
K = b^L \ \text{leaves}, \qquad bL \ \text{distances per descriptor}.
$$
With $b = 10$ and $L = 6$, a descriptor reaches one of $10^6$ words after 60 distance computations.
:::

::: note
[Spatial re-ranking and query expansion]{.tag}
A bag of words ignores geometry. The top of the ranked list is therefore re-ranked by fitting a transformation to the matched words with RANSAC (ch. 3) and counting the inliers (Philbin et al., 2007). Verified results then serve as new queries; this *query expansion* retrieves views that the original query could not reach (Chum et al., 2007). Both steps exploit the rigidity of the instance.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.7 — Product quantisation (Jégou, Douze and Schmid, 2011)]{.tag}
Split $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ into $m$ sub-vectors $x = (x^1, \dots, x^m)$ of dimension $d/m$, and quantise each one with its own codebook of $k^*$ centroids learned by k-means.

The code of $x$ is the $m$-tuple of indices, stored in $m \log_2 k^*$ bits. The product quantiser
$$
q(x) = \big(q_1(x^1), \dots, q_m(x^m)\big)
$$
has an implicit codebook of $(k^*)^m$ centroids, which is never stored.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.8 — Asymmetric distance computation]{.tag}
For a query $y$, which is not quantised, and a database vector $x$ stored by its code,
$$
\|y - q(x)\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^m \big\|y^j - q_j(x^j)\big\|^2 .
$$
After computing $m$ tables of the $k^*$ distances between $y^j$ and the centroids of codebook $j$, each database distance costs $m$ look-ups and additions.

::: proof
The squared Euclidean norm is additive over a partition of the coordinates into blocks, and the $j$-th block of $q(x)$ is the centroid $q_j(x^j)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For SIFT descriptors ($d = 128$) with $m = 8$ and $k^* = 256$, each vector takes 64 bits instead of 4 096 bits in single precision, and the implicit codebook has $2^{64}$ centroids. The code implements k-means and product quantisation on synthetic descriptors that lie near an 8-dimensional subspace.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

def kmeans(X, k, iters=20):
    """Lloyd's algorithm (Proposition 4.2): assign, then recentre."""
    C = X[rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)]
    for _ in range(iters):
        lab = ((X[:, None, :] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1)
        C = np.array([X[lab == j].mean(0) if np.any(lab == j) else C[j] for j in range(k)])
    return C

d, m, ks = 32, 8, 64                   # dimension, sub-vectors, centroids per sub-quantiser
ds = d // m
basis = rng.normal(size=(8, d))        # data near an 8-dimensional subspace, like real descriptors
X = rng.normal(size=(10000, 8)) @ basis + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=(10000, d))
Q = rng.normal(size=(100, 8)) @ basis + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=(100, d))

# One k-means per sub-space; each database vector becomes m one-byte codes
books, codes = [], np.empty((len(X), m), dtype=np.uint8)
for j in range(m):
    sub = X[:, j * ds:(j + 1) * ds]
    books.append(kmeans(sub[:3000], ks))
    codes[:, j] = ((sub[:, None, :] - books[j][None]) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1)

def adc(q):
    """Asymmetric distances: m tables of ks entries, then m look-ups per database vector."""
    tables = [((books[j] - q[j * ds:(j + 1) * ds]) ** 2).sum(1) for j in range(m)]
    return sum(tables[j][codes[:, j]] for j in range(m))

hits = [np.argmin(((X - q) ** 2).sum(1)) in np.argsort(adc(q))[:10] for q in Q]
print(f"memory per vector: {m} bytes instead of {4 * d} bytes (float32)")
print("recall@10 of the exact nearest neighbour:", np.mean(hits))
```

With 8 bytes per vector instead of 128, the exact nearest neighbour is ranked among the first ten for 89 % of the queries. Combined with a coarse quantiser that selects a few cells to scan, this is the IVFADC scheme of Jégou, Douze and Schmid (2011), which later systems scaled to billions of vectors (Johnson, Douze and Jégou, 2019).

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 4
:::

-   Quantising descriptors into visual words turns image matching into text retrieval; Lloyd's algorithm learns the vocabulary.
-   tf-idf weighting and an inverted file make query cost proportional to the lists of the query words, a speed-up of order $K$.
-   Vocabulary trees quantise into $b^L$ words with $bL$ distance computations.
-   Spatial re-ranking and query expansion restore the geometry ignored by the bag of words.
-   Product quantisation compresses vectors to a few bytes and computes distances with table look-ups.
::::

## 5. Category-level recognition: bags of features, sparse coding and dictionary learning {#ch5}

Category-level recognition asks whether an image contains *a* car, any car. Geometric verification no longer applies, because two different cars are not related by a homography. From 2004 to 2012, the dominant answer was statistical: describe the image by the distribution of its local features, and learn a classifier on that description.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Coding and pooling]{.tag}
Let an image give local descriptors $x_1, \dots, x_n$, and let $D = [d_1, \dots, d_K]$ be a dictionary.

-   *Coding* maps each descriptor $x_i$ to a code $\alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}^K$. Hard assignment uses the one-hot vector of the nearest atom.
-   *Pooling* aggregates the codes over a region $S$ of the image: *sum pooling* computes $\sum_{i \in S} \alpha_i$, and *max pooling* takes the maximum over $i \in S$, coordinate by coordinate.

With hard assignment and sum pooling over the whole image, the result is the bag of visual words of Definition 4.3 (Csurka et al., 2004).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Histogram intersection is a positive definite kernel]{.tag}
For histograms $h, h' \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^K$,
$$
k(h, h') = \sum_{j=1}^K \min(h_j, h'_j)
$$
is a positive definite kernel, so it can be used in a support vector machine.

::: proof
-   For $a, b \geq 0$,
$$
\min(a, b) = \int_0^\infty \mathbb{1}[t \leq a]\,\mathbb{1}[t \leq b]\, dt .
$$
-   This is the inner product in $L^2(\mathbb{R}_+)$ of the indicator functions of $[0, a]$ and $[0, b]$, and a kernel of the form $\langle \phi(a), \phi(b) \rangle$ is positive definite.
-   A sum of positive definite kernels is positive definite. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 5.3 — Spatial pyramid matching (Lazebnik, Schmid and Ponce, 2006)]{.tag}
At levels $\ell = 0, \dots, L$, divide the image into $2^\ell \times 2^\ell$ cells and compute a bag of features in each cell. Let $I_\ell$ be the sum over the cells of level $\ell$ of the intersection kernels. The pyramid kernel is
$$
k_L = \frac{1}{2^L}\, I_0 + \sum_{\ell = 1}^{L} \frac{1}{2^{L - \ell + 1}}\, I_\ell ,
$$
so that matches found in finer cells count more. It reinjects the coarse layout of the scene — sky at the top, road at the bottom — into an orderless representation, and it is positive definite as a positive combination of kernels.
:::

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Sparse coding]{.tag}
Given a dictionary $D \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times K}$ with unit-norm columns and $\lambda > 0$, the sparse code of $x$ is
$$
\alpha^\star(x) \in \arg\min_{\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^K}\ \tfrac12\|x - D\alpha\|^2 + \lambda\|\alpha\|_1 .
$$
This is the lasso (Tibshirani, 1996): the $\ell_1$ penalty sets many coordinates exactly to zero, so $x$ is explained by a few atoms. Unlike hard assignment, the code keeps several atoms with graded weights, which reduces the quantisation error.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — Soft-thresholding]{.tag}
In one dimension, the solution of $\min_a \tfrac12 (z - a)^2 + \lambda|a|$ is

::: key
[Key result — soft-thresholding]{.tag}
$$
S_\lambda(z) = \operatorname{sign}(z)\, \max(|z| - \lambda,\ 0).
$$
:::

If $D$ has orthonormal columns, the sparse code is therefore $\alpha^\star = S_\lambda(D^\top x)$, coordinate by coordinate.

::: proof
-   The objective is strictly convex, so $a$ is optimal iff $0 \in a - z + \lambda\, \partial|a|$, where $\partial|a| = \{\operatorname{sign}(a)\}$ if $a \neq 0$ and $[-1, 1]$ if $a = 0$.
-   If $|z| \leq \lambda$, the point $a = 0$ is optimal, since $z \in \lambda[-1, 1]$.
-   If $z > \lambda$, the point $a = z - \lambda > 0$ satisfies $a - z + \lambda = 0$; the case $z < -\lambda$ is symmetric.
-   If $D^\top D = I$, then
$$
\|x - D\alpha\|^2 = \|D^\top x - \alpha\|^2 + \|x\|^2 - \|D^\top x\|^2 ,
$$
and the problem separates over the coordinates. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Algorithm 5.6 — ISTA, iterative shrinkage-thresholding]{.tag}
For a general dictionary, let $L = \|D\|_2^2$, the largest eigenvalue of $D^\top D$, and iterate
$$
\alpha^{t+1} = S_{\lambda/L}\Big(\alpha^t - \tfrac{1}{L}\, D^\top (D\alpha^t - x)\Big).
$$
Each iteration is a gradient step on the smooth term, which is $L$-smooth (Proposition 0.6), followed by the exact minimisation of the $\ell_1$ term (Proposition 5.5). The objective converges at the rate $O(1/t)$, and at the rate $O(1/t^2)$ for the accelerated variant FISTA (Beck and Teboulle, 2009).
:::

::: def
[Definition 5.7 — Dictionary learning]{.tag}
Given training descriptors $x_1, \dots, x_N$, learn the dictionary together with the codes:
$$
\min_{D \in \mathcal{C},\ \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N}\ \sum_{i=1}^N \tfrac12\|x_i - D\alpha_i\|^2 + \lambda\|\alpha_i\|_1 ,
$$
where $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of matrices whose columns have norm at most 1. Without this constraint, scaling $D$ up and the codes down would drive the penalty to zero.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.8 — Alternate minimisation]{.tag}
The objective of Definition 5.7 is not jointly convex, but it is convex in the codes for a fixed $D$, and convex in $D \in \mathcal{C}$ for fixed codes. Alternating exact minimisations over the two blocks therefore produces a non-increasing sequence of objective values.

::: proof
-   For fixed $D$, each term is a lasso problem, convex in $\alpha_i$.
-   For fixed codes, $D \mapsto \sum_i \|x_i - D\alpha_i\|^2$ is a convex quadratic, and $\mathcal{C}$ is convex.
-   Each block step minimises the objective over its block, so it cannot increase it.
-   Joint convexity fails already in dimension one: with $x = 1$, the loss $(x - D\alpha)^2$ vanishes at $(1, 1)$ and at $(-1, -1)$ but equals 1 at their midpoint. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

K-SVD updates the atoms one at a time with a rank-one SVD (Aharon, Elad and Bruckstein, 2006). Online dictionary learning processes one mini-batch at a time and scales to millions of patches (Mairal, Bach, Ponce and Sapiro, 2009). Dictionaries learned on natural image patches resemble oriented edge detectors, like the receptive fields of the primary visual cortex (Olshausen and Field, 1996).

Sparse codes, max-pooled over a spatial pyramid and fed to a *linear* SVM, matched non-linear kernel SVMs on bags of features at a fraction of the cost (Yang et al., 2009). The code compares these representations on the 8 × 8 digits bundled with scikit-learn, using all 4 × 4 patches as local descriptors.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

imgs, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
imgs = imgs.reshape(-1, 8, 8) / 16.0
# all 4 x 4 patches (5 x 5 positions), centred: shape (n, 25, 16)
P = np.stack([imgs[:, i:i + 4, j:j + 4].reshape(len(imgs), 16)
              for i in range(5) for j in range(5)], 1)
P = P - P.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
cell = np.array([(i > 2) * 2 + (j > 2) for i in range(5) for j in range(5)])  # 2 x 2 grid

def pyramid(F, pool):
    """Level 0 (whole image) + level 1 (2 x 2 cells) pooling of patch codes F: (n, 25, K)."""
    return np.concatenate([pool(F, 1)] + [pool(F[:, cell == c], 1) for c in range(4)], 1)

def ista(X, D, lam, iters=50):
    """Lasso codes for every row of X (Algorithm 5.6), step 1/L with L = ||D||_2^2."""
    L = np.linalg.norm(D, 2) ** 2
    A = np.zeros((len(X), D.shape[1]))
    for _ in range(iters):
        Z = A - (A @ D.T - X) @ D / L
        A = np.sign(Z) * np.maximum(np.abs(Z) - lam / L, 0)          # soft-thresholding
    return A

K, flat = 32, P.reshape(-1, 16)
train = flat[rng.choice(len(flat), 2000, replace=False)]
# (a) bag of features: k-means vocabulary, hard assignment, sum pooling
C = train[rng.choice(len(train), K, replace=False)]
for _ in range(20):
    lab = ((train[:, None] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1)
    C = np.array([train[lab == k].mean(0) if np.any(lab == k) else C[k] for k in range(K)])
H = np.eye(K)[((P[..., None, :] - C) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(-1)]       # one-hot codes
# (b) sparse coding: alternate ISTA codes and least-squares dictionary updates
D = train[:K].T / np.linalg.norm(train[:K], axis=1)
for _ in range(5):
    A = ista(train, D, lam=0.05)
    D = np.linalg.lstsq(A, train, rcond=None)[0].T
    D /= np.maximum(np.linalg.norm(D, axis=0), 1e-8)
S = np.abs(ista(flat, D, lam=0.05)).reshape(len(imgs), 25, K)

feats = {"raw pixels": imgs.reshape(len(imgs), -1),
         "BoF, sum pooling, level 0": H.sum(1),
         "BoF, spatial pyramid": pyramid(H, np.sum),
         "sparse codes, max pooling, pyramid": pyramid(S, np.max)}
for name, F in feats.items():
    F = F / np.linalg.norm(F, axis=1, keepdims=True)                 # L2-normalise
    Ftr, Fte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(F, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)
    acc = LinearSVC(C=1.0, max_iter=20000).fit(Ftr, ytr).score(Fte, yte)
    print(f"{name:36s} test accuracy {acc:.3f}")
```

The orderless bag of features loses information (88.0 % against 96.3 % for raw pixels). The spatial pyramid recovers it (96.1 %), and sparse codes with max pooling do best (98.9 %).

::: note
[VLAD and Fisher vectors]{.tag}
Hard assignment keeps only counts, the zeroth-order statistics of the descriptors in each cell. VLAD stores first-order statistics, the sum of the residuals $x_i - c_k$ of the descriptors assigned to each centroid, in a vector of dimension $Kd$ (Jégou et al., 2010). Fisher vectors add second-order statistics under a Gaussian mixture model (Perronnin, Sánchez and Mensink, 2010). With power and L2 normalisation, they were the state of the art for large-scale image classification just before convolutional networks (Sánchez et al., 2013).
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 5
:::

-   Category-level pipelines code local descriptors on a dictionary, pool the codes over regions, and train a classifier.
-   Histogram intersection is positive definite; spatial pyramids add coarse layout to orderless bags.
-   Sparse coding solves a lasso per descriptor, by soft-thresholding iterations (ISTA); dictionaries are learned by alternate minimisation.
-   Richer codes (sparse codes, VLAD, Fisher vectors) let linear classifiers match kernel machines.
::::

## 6. Neural networks and optimisation methods {#ch6}

The pipelines of ch. 5 learn only their last stage, the classifier; descriptors, coding and pooling are designed by hand. Neural networks learn every stage jointly, by gradient descent on a loss computed from the labels. This chapter covers the model, the computation of its gradient and the optimisers.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Multilayer perceptron and cross-entropy]{.tag}
A multilayer perceptron with $L$ layers computes $a_0 = x$ and, for $\ell = 1, \dots, L$,
$$
z_\ell = W_\ell\, a_{\ell - 1} + b_\ell, \qquad a_\ell = \sigma(z_\ell),
$$
with a non-linearity $\sigma$ applied coordinatewise — usually the ReLU $\sigma(u) = \max(u, 0)$ — and none on the last layer. For $C$ classes, the output $z_L \in \mathbb{R}^C$ is turned into probabilities by the softmax, and the loss for the true class $y$ is the cross-entropy:
$$
p = \operatorname{softmax}(z_L), \qquad \mathcal{L} = -\log p_y .
$$
:::

One hidden layer already suffices to approximate any continuous function on a compact set: Cybenko (1989) and Hornik (1991) prove it for sigmoidal and bounded activations, and Leshno et al. (1993) for every non-polynomial one, the ReLU included. Depth makes such approximations far more economical, and it is what makes features reusable across tasks.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Gradient of the softmax cross-entropy]{.tag}
With $Y = e_y$ the one-hot encoding of the true class,
$$
\nabla_{z_L} \mathcal{L} = p - Y .
$$

::: proof
$\mathcal{L} = -z_{L,y} + \log \sum_c e^{z_{L,c}}$, so the derivative with respect to $z_{L,c}$ is
$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_{L,c}} = -\mathbb{1}[c = y] + \frac{e^{z_{L,c}}}{\sum_{c'} e^{z_{L,c'}}} = p_c - Y_c .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Backpropagation]{.tag}
Let $\delta_\ell = \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial z_\ell$. Then $\delta_L = p - Y$ by Proposition 6.2, and for $\ell = L, \dots, 1$:
$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_\ell} = \delta_\ell\, a_{\ell-1}^\top, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b_\ell} = \delta_\ell, \qquad \delta_{\ell - 1} = \big(W_\ell^\top \delta_\ell\big) \odot \sigma'(z_{\ell - 1}).
$$
All the gradients are obtained in one backward pass, whose cost is of the same order as the forward pass.

::: proof
-   $z_\ell$ depends linearly on $W_\ell$: the derivative of $z_{\ell,i}$ with respect to $W_{\ell,ij}$ is $a_{\ell-1,j}$. The chain rule gives the first two formulas.
-   $z_\ell = W_\ell\, \sigma(z_{\ell-1}) + b_\ell$ has Jacobian $J = W_\ell \operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_{\ell-1}))$ with respect to $z_{\ell-1}$. The chain rule $\delta_{\ell-1} = J^\top \delta_\ell$ gives the recursion.
-   Each step costs one product by $W_\ell^\top$ and one outer product, the same order as the product $W_\ell a_{\ell-1}$ of the forward pass. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Reverse-mode automatic differentiation, as in PyTorch, applies the same recursion to any computation graph.

::: def
[Definition 6.4 — Stochastic gradient methods]{.tag}
Let $f(\theta) = \frac1N \sum_i \mathcal{L}_i(\theta)$ be the training loss. A mini-batch $B$ of size $b$, drawn uniformly, gives an unbiased estimate $g = \frac1b \sum_{i \in B} \nabla \mathcal{L}_i(\theta)$ of the gradient.

-   *SGD*: $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, g$, with learning rate $\eta$.
-   *Momentum*: $v \leftarrow \mu v - \eta g$, then $\theta \leftarrow \theta + v$, with $\mu \approx 0.9$.
-   *Adam* (Kingma and Ba, 2015) keeps running averages $m$ of $g$ and $s$ of $g^2$, with rates $\beta_1 = 0.9$ and $\beta_2 = 0.999$.

    It corrects their bias at step $t$, and updates each coordinate by
$$
\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \frac{m / (1 - \beta_1^t)}{\sqrt{s / (1 - \beta_2^t)} + \epsilon} .
$$

AdamW applies weight decay directly to $\theta$ rather than through $g$ (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.5 — SGD on a smooth non-convex loss]{.tag}
Assume that $f$ is bounded below by $f^\star$, that $\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, and that the stochastic gradients satisfy $\mathbb{E}\|g - \nabla f(\theta)\|^2 \leq \sigma^2$.

Then SGD with a constant step $\eta \leq 1/L$ satisfies, after $T$ steps,
$$
\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \mathbb{E}\,\|\nabla f(\theta_t)\|^2 \ \leq\ \frac{2\,(f(\theta_0) - f^\star)}{\eta T} + L \eta \sigma^2 .
$$

::: proof
-   The descent lemma (Proposition 0.6) with $\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta g_t$ gives
$$
f(\theta_{t+1}) \leq f(\theta_t) - \eta\, \nabla f(\theta_t)^\top g_t + \frac{L\eta^2}{2}\|g_t\|^2 .
$$
-   Conditionally on $\theta_t$, the gradient estimate is unbiased, $\mathbb{E}[g_t] = \nabla f(\theta_t)$, and its second moment is bounded:
$$
\mathbb{E}\|g_t\|^2 = \|\nabla f(\theta_t)\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|g_t - \nabla f(\theta_t)\|^2 \leq \|\nabla f(\theta_t)\|^2 + \sigma^2 .
$$
-   Since $\eta \leq 1/L$, we have $-\eta + L\eta^2/2 \leq -\eta/2$, hence
$$
\mathbb{E} f(\theta_{t+1}) \leq \mathbb{E} f(\theta_t) - \frac{\eta}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(\theta_t)\|^2 + \frac{L\eta^2\sigma^2}{2} .
$$
-   Sum over $t = 0, \dots, T-1$, use $f(\theta_T) \geq f^\star$, and divide by $\eta T/2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The first term is the rate of deterministic gradient descent; the second is a noise floor proportional to the step. This explains learning-rate decay schedules, and the effect of the batch size: averaging $b$ independent per-example gradients divides their variance by $b$ (Bottou, Curtis and Nocedal, 2018).

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.6 — He initialisation]{.tag}
Consider a ReLU layer $z_\ell = W_\ell\, \sigma(z_{\ell-1})$ with $n$ inputs. Assume the weights are i.i.d., centred, of variance $v$, independent of $z_{\ell-1}$, and that the coordinates of $z_{\ell-1}$ are identically distributed and symmetric around 0. Then
$$
\operatorname{Var}(z_{\ell,i}) = \frac{n v}{2}\, \operatorname{Var}(z_{\ell-1,j}) ,
$$
so the choice $v = 2/n$ keeps the scale of the pre-activations constant through depth (He et al., 2015).

::: proof
-   $z_{\ell,i} = \sum_j W_{ij}\, a_j$ with independent centred weights, so
$$
\operatorname{Var}(z_{\ell,i}) = n v\, \mathbb{E}[a_j^2] .
$$
-   For $z$ symmetric around 0,
$$
\mathbb{E}[\max(z, 0)^2] = \tfrac12\, \mathbb{E}[z^2] = \tfrac12 \operatorname{Var}(z) .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Regularisation and normalisation]{.tag}
-   *Weight decay* adds $\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|^2$ to the loss.
-   *Data augmentation* — random crops, flips, colour changes — encodes invariances that the model should have; in vision it is the most effective regulariser.
-   *Dropout* sets each hidden unit to zero with probability $p$ during training (Srivastava et al., 2014).
-   *Batch normalisation* standardises each channel with the mean and variance of the mini-batch, then applies a learned affine map (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015). It allows much larger learning rates.
:::

The code implements Theorem 6.3 in NumPy, checks it against a finite difference, and trains with momentum on the two-moons data set.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X, y = make_moons(400, noise=0.2, random_state=0)
Y = np.eye(2)[y]                                      # one-hot targets

def init(sizes):                                      # He initialisation (Proposition 6.6)
    return [(rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / a), (a, b)), np.zeros(b)) for a, b in zip(sizes, sizes[1:])]

def forward(params, X):
    acts = [X]
    for i, (W, b) in enumerate(params):
        z = acts[-1] @ W + b
        acts.append(np.maximum(z, 0) if i < len(params) - 1 else z)
    return acts

def loss_and_grads(params, X, Y):
    acts = forward(params, X)
    z = acts[-1] - acts[-1].max(1, keepdims=True)
    p = np.exp(z) / np.exp(z).sum(1, keepdims=True)  # softmax
    loss = -np.mean(np.sum(Y * np.log(p), 1))
    delta = (p - Y) / len(X)                          # Proposition 6.2
    grads = []
    for i in reversed(range(len(params))):            # backward pass (Theorem 6.3)
        grads.append((acts[i].T @ delta, delta.sum(0)))
        if i > 0:
            delta = (delta @ params[i][0].T) * (acts[i] > 0)
    return loss, grads[::-1]

params = init([2, 32, 32, 2])
loss, grads = loss_and_grads(params, X, Y)
eps = 1e-6
params[0][0][0, 0] += eps                             # finite-difference check of one weight
loss_eps, _ = loss_and_grads(params, X, Y)
params[0][0][0, 0] -= eps
print(f"backprop {grads[0][0][0, 0]:.6f}   finite difference {(loss_eps - loss) / eps:.6f}")

vel = [(np.zeros_like(W), np.zeros_like(b)) for W, b in params]
for step in range(2000):                              # mini-batch SGD with momentum 0.9
    idx = rng.choice(len(X), 32, replace=False)
    _, grads = loss_and_grads(params, X[idx], Y[idx])
    for (W, b), (gW, gb), (vW, vb) in zip(params, grads, vel):
        vW *= 0.9; vW -= 0.05 * gW; W += vW
        vb *= 0.9; vb -= 0.05 * gb; b += vb
print("training accuracy:", (forward(params, X)[-1].argmax(1) == y).mean())
```

The backpropagated derivative and the finite difference agree to six decimals, and the network separates the two moons with 97.5 % training accuracy.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 6
:::

-   The gradient of the softmax cross-entropy with respect to the logits is $p - Y$; backpropagation propagates it through the layers at the cost of one forward pass.
-   SGD converges to stationary points of smooth non-convex losses, up to a noise floor proportional to the step (Theorem 6.5).
-   Momentum and Adam accelerate training; He initialisation keeps activations at a constant scale.
-   Data augmentation, weight decay, dropout and batch normalisation control overfitting and ease optimisation.
::::

## 7. Convolutional neural networks for visual recognition {#ch7}

A fully connected layer from a 224 × 224 colour image to the 112 × 112 × 64 feature map of a standard first layer would need about $10^{11}$ weights (Example 7.2). Convolutional networks build in two properties of images, locality and the equivalence of positions. Since 2012 they have dominated recognition (Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, 2012).

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Convolutional layer]{.tag}
A convolutional layer maps an input $X$ with $C_{\text{in}}$ channels to an output $Y$ with $C_{\text{out}}$ channels:
$$
Y_{c'}(x) = b_{c'} + \sum_{c=1}^{C_{\text{in}}} \sum_{u \in \{-r, \dots, r\}^2} W_{c',c}(u)\, X_c(s x + u),
$$
with kernel size $k = 2r + 1$ and stride $s$. With a padding of $p$ pixels, an input of width $n$ gives an output of width
$$
\Big\lfloor \frac{n + 2p - k}{s} \Big\rfloor + 1 ,
$$
and the layer has $k^2 C_{\text{in}} C_{\text{out}} + C_{\text{out}}$ parameters, whatever the size of the image.
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.2 — Counting]{.tag}
Apply to a $224 \times 224 \times 3$ image 64 filters of size $7 \times 7$, with stride 2 and padding 3, as in the first layer of a ResNet.

-   Output width: $\lfloor (224 + 6 - 7)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 112$, so the output is $112 \times 112 \times 64$.
-   Parameters: $7 \cdot 7 \cdot 3 \cdot 64$ weights and 64 biases, that is, 9 472.

A fully connected layer between the same input (150 528 values) and output (802 816 values) would need
$$
150\,528 \times 802\,816 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{11} \ \text{weights}.
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.3 — Equivariance and invariance]{.tag}
Let $\tau_a$ translate every channel by $a$, with circular boundary conditions and stride 1.

1.  A convolutional layer followed by a pointwise non-linearity commutes with $\tau_a$, and so does any stack $\Phi$ of such layers: $\Phi(\tau_a X) = \tau_a \Phi(X)$.
2.  Global average or max pooling of the output is invariant to translations of the input.

::: proof
1.  Each output channel is a sum of convolutions plus a constant, and commutes with $\tau_a$ (Proposition 0.2). A pointwise map $\sigma$ satisfies $\sigma(\tau_a X) = \tau_a\sigma(X)$. A composition of maps that commute with $\tau_a$ commutes with $\tau_a$.
2.  The mean and the maximum over all positions do not depend on the order of the positions, and $\tau_a$ only permutes them. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Strides and pooling break exact equivariance: a one-pixel shift of the input can change the output of a strided layer, a form of aliasing (Zhang, 2019). Recognition networks are therefore only approximately shift-invariant, and data augmentation fills the gap.

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.4 — Receptive field]{.tag}
Stack layers with kernel sizes $k_\ell$ and strides $s_\ell$, and let $j_\ell = s_1 \cdots s_\ell$ be the distance, in input pixels, between adjacent units of layer $\ell$ (with $j_0 = 1$).

The receptive field $r_\ell$ — the width of the input region that can influence one unit of layer $\ell$ — satisfies

::: key
[Key result — the receptive field recursion]{.tag}
$$
r_0 = 1, \qquad r_\ell = r_{\ell - 1} + (k_\ell - 1)\, j_{\ell - 1} .
$$
:::


::: proof
A unit of layer $\ell$ sees $k_\ell$ adjacent units of layer $\ell - 1$, whose centres are $j_{\ell-1}$ input pixels apart; these centres span $(k_\ell - 1)\, j_{\ell-1}$ pixels.

Each of these units sees $r_{\ell-1}$ pixels around its centre, so the union has width $r_{\ell-1} + (k_\ell - 1)\, j_{\ell-1}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Three $3 \times 3$ convolutions with stride 1 have the receptive field $1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7$ of a single $7 \times 7$ layer. They use $27C^2$ weights instead of $49C^2$ for $C$ channels, and three non-linearities instead of one: this is the design principle of VGG networks (Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015).

::: def
[Definition 7.5 — Residual block (He et al., 2016)]{.tag}
A residual block computes
$$
x_{\ell + 1} = x_\ell + F_\ell(x_\ell),
$$
where $F_\ell$ is a small stack of convolutions, batch normalisations and ReLUs. A ResNet chains dozens of such blocks.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.6 — Residual connections carry the gradient]{.tag}
For a chain of residual blocks from $x_\ell$ to $x_L$, with gradients written as row vectors,
$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_\ell} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_L} \Big(I + \frac{\partial F_{L-1}}{\partial x_{L-1}}\Big) \cdots \Big(I + \frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial x_\ell}\Big).
$$
Expanding the product, the gradient contains the direct term $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial x_L$, which no weight can attenuate.

::: proof
Apply the chain rule, with the Jacobian $I + \partial F_m / \partial x_m$ of each block. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Architectures and transfer]{.tag}
-   LeNet-5 read handwritten digits with alternating convolutional and subsampling layers (LeCun et al., 1998).
-   AlexNet scaled the recipe to ImageNet with ReLUs, dropout, data augmentation and GPUs (Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, 2012).
-   VGG networks stacked $3 \times 3$ convolutions, and ResNets trained 152 layers thanks to residual connections.
-   Vision transformers cut the image into $16 \times 16$ patches treated as the tokens of a transformer; with enough pre-training data they match or exceed CNNs (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021).

Features of a network pre-trained on ImageNet transfer to other tasks: retraining only the last layers works with few labelled images (Oquab et al., 2014).
:::

The code trains a small CNN with global average pooling on the 8 × 8 digits, and checks Proposition 7.3 on a circular convolution.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
torch.manual_seed(0)

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X = torch.tensor(X / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1, 8, 8)
y = torch.tensor(y)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)
```
